displayQuote: I do not believe in God, because I believe in man

meta.title: Who really said "I do not believe in God, because I believe in man"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, Emma Goldman wrote it. Her memoir Living My Life records the line as her reply to a questioner in a Detroit church; the Emma Goldman Papers chronology dates the evening to 19 November 1897.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I do not believe in God, because I believe in man'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Emma Goldman — verified in Living My Life, ch. 16. But the internet keeps dropping the second sentence, the one with teeth.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Goldman set the line down herself in Living My Life, Volume One, Chapter 16 (Alfred A. Knopf, 1931), recording her reply to a woman who stood up in a Detroit church and demanded to know whether she believed in God. The wording is confirmed verbatim in the memoir text — and it does not stop where the internet stops it: the next sentence is “Whatever his mistakes, man has for thousands of years past been working to undo the botched job your God has made.”

source.heading: The source, confirmed

docMeta.dd: Living My Life, Volume One, Chapter 16
Her reply from the pulpit of Detroit’s People’s Tabernacle, 19 November 1897
Confirmed verbatim in two independent full-text transcriptions

source.excerpt: “Ladies and gentlemen,” I began, “I came here to avoid as much as possible treading on your corns. I had intended to deal only with the basic issue of economics that dictates our lives from the cradle to the grave, regardless of our religion or moral beliefs. I see now that it was a mistake. If one enters a battle, he cannot be squeamish about a few corns. Here, then, are my answers: I do not believe in God, because I believe in man. Whatever his mistakes, man has for thousands of years past been working to undo the botched job your God has made.”
trail: The sentence appears word for word in Living My Life, Volume One, Chapter 16 ↗, inside Goldman’s account of the questions shouted at her after she finished speaking in the Tabernacle.
A second, independent transcription of the whole memoir at The Anarchist Library ↗ carries the identical wording, which rules out a single transcriber’s error.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the passage with the same memoir source, citing p. 207 of the 1931 edition and Annie Laurie Gaylor’s Women Without Superstition, though it dates the speech to 1898.

The Emma Goldman Papers chronology, mirrored at libcom ↗, records that on 19 November 1897 Goldman “speaks at the People’s Tabernacle despite opposition from the congregation” and that the deacons then asked for the pastor’s resignation — matching the memoir scene.
source.excerptNote: What follows in the memoir: “The house went frantic.” Because the book was written in France and published in 1931, this is Goldman’s own account of the 1897 evening rather than a transcript taken in the room.

source.rightsNote: Living My Life was published in the United States in 1931 by Alfred A. Knopf, in two volumes. A US book of that vintage kept its copyright only if the registration was renewed in its 28th year, and no renewal for this one has been found: Wikisource ↗ hosts the complete text under the PD-US-no-renewal tag, the Online Books Page ↗ lists the 1931 Knopf edition as freely readable in full view at HathiTrust, and Dover reprinted the book unabridged in 1970. On that reading the work has been in the US public domain since 1 January 1960; Goldman died in 1940, so the life-plus-70 term has also run out elsewhere. One caveat we owe you: this rests on the absence of a renewal record in the published indexes, not on a search we were able to run ourselves against the Copyright Office renewal database.

author.name: Emma Goldman
author.heading: Who was Emma Goldman?
author.metaLine: 1869–1940 · Anarchist orator, writer and editor of Mother Earth
author.bio: Born in Kovno in 1869 and dead in Toronto in 1940, Emma Goldman was the most notorious anarchist in America — a factory worker turned lecturer who toured relentlessly on anarchism, free speech, atheism, birth control and free love, and who was deported to Russia in 1919. She founded and edited the journal Mother Earth and wrote Anarchism and Other Essays (1910) and The Social Significance of the Modern Drama (1914). Her two-volume autobiography Living My Life, written in Saint-Tropez after her disillusionment with the Bolsheviks, is where this sentence is documented.

misattribution.heading: The attribution holds. The quotation doesn’t.
misattribution.intro: This is not a fake — it is a real Goldman sentence that gets trimmed, misdated and slightly misworded on its way around the internet. Three things to watch for:

items.why: The line is almost always served as the bare aphorism. QuotePark ↗ headlines it as “I do not believe in God, because I believe in man.” and files the rest under “Context.” The sentence Goldman actually caused a riot with is the second one, about undoing “the botched job your God has made.”

Goodreads ↗ prints “for thousands of years been working” and lowercases “god,” with no book or date named at all. The memoir reads “for thousands of years past been working” and capitalises “your God.”

items.who: Wikiquote, and everyone who copies it
items.why: Wikiquote ↗ cites the exchange to a speech in Detroit in 1898, and aggregators reproduce that citation word for word. The Emma Goldman Papers chronology instead places her People’s Tabernacle appearance on 19 November 1897 ↗, at the end of her 1897 tour.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are genuinely Goldman’s, written by her and printed in Living My Life, Volume One, Chapter 16 ↗. Quote them whole, and get the year right.

context.heading: The night the church went frantic
lead: The Reverend Dr. H. S. McCowan had heard Goldman lecture in German and invited her into his own pulpit so his congregation could hear America’s most notorious anarchist in English. Detroit’s papers ran headlines about a congregational church being turned into a “hotbed of anarchy and free love,” and members and committees besieged him to withdraw. He refused: “A church that refuses the right of expression to the most unpopular person or creed is no place for me.”

Goldman, by her own account, deliberately kept the hour-long lecture to economics so that McCowan would not pay for her. It worked — until the applause died and an elderly woman rose “belligerently” to ask whether Miss Goldman believed in God. Goldman told the minister she would have to answer straight from the shoulder. He said: “So be it.” The line quoted today is what came next, and according to the memoir the room erupted — “Blasphemy! Heretic! Sinner!” McCowan resigned from the church.
context.detailsSummary: What else she said that night
detailsBody: The same volley of questions asked whether she favoured killing all rulers. Goldman answered that some potentates she would kill by any means at her disposal — “Ignorance, Superstition, and Bigotry — the most sinister and tyrannical rulers on earth.”

One honest caveat about the scene, not the sentence: Living My Life was written in France and published in 1931, so the Detroit exchange is Goldman’s recollection of an evening in 1897, not a stenographic record of it. No period transcript of the reply was located for this page. The sentence is verified as Goldman’s writing; the 1897 delivery rests on her own account.
context.pull: I shall have to answer these people straight from the shoulder.

sourcesVerified.claim: Living My Life, Volume One, Chapter 16 contains verbatim: "I do not believe in God, because I believe in man. Whatever his mistakes, man has for thousands of years past been working to undo the botched job your God has made.", spoken in reply to a questioner at a Detroit church where Rev. Dr. McCowan presided; the house went frantic and McCowan afterwards resigned.
An independent full text of Living My Life carries the identical sentence and surrounding passage.

Wikiquote lists the quote with the fuller passage, sourced to "Responding to audience questions during a speech in Detroit (1898); as recounted in Living My Life (1931), p. 207; quoted by Annie Laurie Gaylor in Women Without Superstition, p. 382".

The Emma Goldman Papers chronology states that in mid-November 1897 Goldman lectured four times in Detroit and that "On Nov. 19, Goldman speaks at the People's Tabernacle despite opposition from the congregation; the event is sensationalized in the press", after which the deacons and members requested the pastor's resignation. The page notes the chronology was taken from the Emma Goldman Papers at Berkeley, no longer online.

Wikipedia states that Living My Life was published in two volumes, 1931 (Alfred A. Knopf) and 1934 (Garden City Publishing Company), and was written in Saint-Tropez, France. The volume dating is NOT relied on here: the Wikipedia article on Emma Goldman gives 1931 and 1935, and the Online Books Page and first-edition dealer records both describe a two-volume Knopf set dated 1931, with Garden City 1934 as a later reprint.

The Online Books Page lists "Living My Life (2 volumes; New York: Alfred A. Knopf Inc., 1931)" as freely readable (HTML at pitzer.edu, page images at HathiTrust), with the Garden City Publishing Company 1934 printing listed separately as an alternate edition. HathiTrust full view of a 1931 US book follows a renewal check.

English Wikisource hosts the complete text of Living My Life under the PD-US-no-renewal tag: "This work is in the public domain in the United States because it was legally published within the United States ... before 1964, and copyright was not renewed." Corroborated by Dover Publications' unabridged 1970 reprint (archive.org item livingmylife02gold, publisher "New York, Dover Publications", 1970, "Reprint of the 1931 ed."). The Stanford Copyright Renewal Database could not be queried directly - it serves a CAPTCHA to automated requests - so the non-renewal finding rests on these published indexes.

Emma Goldman was born 27 June 1869 in Kaunas (Kovno) and died 14 May 1940 in Toronto; her notable works include Anarchism and Other Essays (1910), Living My Life (1931) and The Social Significance of the Modern Drama (1914).

Goodreads prints the quote as "...man has for thousands of years been working to undo the botched job your god has made" - omitting "past" and lowercasing "god" - attributed only to Emma Goldman with no work or date.
QuotePark headlines the bare one-sentence form and reproduces the Wikiquote citation dating the Detroit speech to 1898, with the rest of the passage relegated to a "Context" note.
